title: Book 7 — Polymnia, Chapter 209
paragraphs: Hearing this, Xerxes could not guess the truth of the matter — that they were preparing to die and to deal out death to the enemy as far as they could. It seemed to him that they were simply acting ridiculously. So he sent for Demaratos son of Ariston, who was in his camp, and when he came, Xerxes questioned him about each of these things, wanting to discover what the Lacedaemonians were doing. Demaratos said: “You heard from my own mouth earlier, when we were setting out to march against Greece, what sort of men these are; and having heard it, you made me a laughingstock, because I told you what I foresaw would come to pass. For to me, O king, the greatest of all ends is to speak the truth continually before you. Hear me now too: these men have come to fight us for the passage, and this is what they are preparing to do. They have a custom that whenever they are about to risk their lives, they attend to the arrangement of their hair. Be assured, however, that if you overcome these men and the rest who remain behind in Sparta, there is no other race of men that will withstand your onset, O king, or raise hands against you; for you are now about to fight the noblest kingdom and city among the Greeks, and their best men.” To Xerxes what was said seemed utterly incredible, and he asked again how it was possible that so few would fight against his host. Demaratos said, “O king, treat me as a liar if you do not find that these things come to pass as I say.”
